bp: Many real systems leave behind traces of spread without revealing the pathways that carried the spread. A rumor may appear in several communities, a behavior may show up across groups of users, or a signal may move through related networks, but the observer may only see who ended up affected, not every contact that caused it. This paper serves the task of reconstructing those hidden pathways. The object being inferred is a diffusion network: a set of entities and the possible routes along which something can pass. The important twist is that the paper does not assume one richly observed network. It starts from several networks whose spreading processes look related, while each separate network has too little evidence to recover its structure confidently. The practical need is therefore shared reconstruction: use weak clues from several similar spreading systems so each one can be inferred better than it could be alone.
wh: The hard part is that spread observations are indirect evidence. Seeing the final or observed diffusion results tells us that influence, infection, information, or another signal traveled somehow, but many different network structures could have produced similar outcomes. If there is abundant observation data for one network, repeated spreading cases can gradually rule out some hidden routes and support others. The abstract says the real setting is often worse: each individual network has limited observable data. That means the evidence inside one task is thin, and a method that treats the task alone can mistake random gaps for real missing links or random coincidences for real routes. At the same time, the networks are only similar, not necessarily identical. Borrowing too aggressively from other networks could erase real differences. The central tension is therefore between isolation and over-sharing: each network needs help from related networks, but it must still keep its own structure.
naive: A smart beginner would infer each diffusion network separately. For each network, they would collect its observed diffusion results, search for a structure that could explain those results, and output that structure without looking at the other networks. This is natural because each network is a separate object: its nodes and links may describe a particular community, platform, region, or setting. The failure is the assumption named in the abstract: enough observation data must be available for every individual inference task. When each network has only a small number of observed spreading results, the separate estimate is underfed. It can fit the few visible cases while missing the hidden structure that would become clear only after more observations. It also wastes the clue that the networks have similar structures.
ap: The core idea is to turn several weak reconstruction problems into one shared reconstruction process. Instead of solving network A, then network B, then network C as isolated jobs, the method updates the inferred structures for all diffusion networks in an iterative cycle. After one network receives an initial estimate from its own observed spreading results, that estimate can be adjusted using what has been learned from the other similar networks. Then those updated estimates become better evidence for the next round. In plain terms, each task is allowed to say, "my observations are sparse, but related tasks suggest which hidden routes are plausible." The paper's central move is not merely averaging all networks together. It is an alternating update strategy that repeatedly uses similarity between networks while still maintaining separate inference results for each diffusion network.
mech: The input is a collection of diffusion-network inference tasks. For each task, the visible data consists of observed diffusion results, which are outcomes of spreading processes rather than the complete route map itself. The desired output is an inferred underlying structure for each network: which connections likely allowed the spread. A separate method would estimate each structure using only its own observations. This paper instead runs a joint loop. First, each network has a current inferred structure, likely initialized from the evidence available inside that task. Next, the method examines the similarity among the networks. Similarity here means that the hidden structures are expected to share patterns, so evidence about one route pattern in one network can make a related route pattern more plausible in another. The strategy then updates the inference result for one or more networks by combining its own observed diffusion evidence with information carried from the other current inferred networks. After all networks have been updated, the process repeats. Each round should improve or at least not worsen the joint inference objective, because the abstract states a monotonicity guarantee. The loop stops when repeated updates converge, meaning later rounds no longer change the inferred structures in a meaningful way. The final output is a set of network estimates, one per task, produced by shared evidence rather than isolated fitting.
math: The main mathematical idea is joint estimation under shared structure. Estimation means using partial observations to choose the hidden object that best explains them. Here the hidden object is a network, and the observations are diffusion results. Joint estimation means the choice for one network is not made alone; it is coupled to choices for other networks because the networks are assumed to be similar. A second idea is similarity as a controlled borrowing rule. Similarity compresses a rich structural comparison into a guide for how much one task should learn from another. That is useful because sparse observations create uncertainty, but it is risky because a single number or score can hide important differences between networks. A third idea is iterative optimization, meaning the method defines a measure of how good the current inferred networks are and repeatedly updates the controllable objects, the network estimates, to improve that measure. The monotonicity guarantee says each step moves in a non-worsening direction according to that measure. Convergence says the process reaches a stable point rather than cycling forever. These guarantees matter because a shared update loop could otherwise bounce between tasks: one network changes another, which changes the first back. The tradeoff is accuracy versus over-coupling: borrowing more information reduces data scarcity, but only if structural similarity is real enough to justify the borrowing.
dots: This paper belongs with the repo's graph-learning family because the answer is not inside one record; it is in the pattern of connections that lets evidence travel. It also connects to the social-networks and influence family, where rumors, opinions, events, or behaviors move through linked people or accounts and the hidden question is who could have affected whom. Unlike papers that simulate a known spread process, this one works backward from observed diffusion results to recover the network that may have produced them. It also connects to probability, because limited observations leave several possible hidden structures plausible, and repeated evidence across related tasks should change those beliefs. Finally, it connects to optimization: the method repeatedly updates inferred networks and relies on monotonicity and convergence to make that updating disciplined. Neighboring papers in the same batch include graph transferability and graph contrastive learning, which also ask how structural evidence can be reused or distinguished across graph settings.
ww: The method should improve over isolated inference because the separate tasks contain complementary evidence. Suppose each network has only a few observed diffusion results. In one network, a certain hidden route may be weakly suggested but not certain. In another similar network, a related route pattern may be clearer. If the networks truly share structural habits, then the second task supplies a reason to trust the first task's weak clue more than before. Repeating this across all networks lets small pieces of evidence reinforce one another. The iterative design matters because the best shared signal is not available at the start; it becomes cleaner as each network's estimate improves. Monotonic updating matters because shared learning can easily become unstable if each task keeps pulling others in changing directions. A guaranteed non-worsening process gives the method a reason to keep updating until it settles. In everyday terms, several partial maps can help repair each other when they describe similar terrain, as long as the repair process checks each map against its own observations and does not force all maps to become identical.
po: The payoff is better recovery of diffusion-network structures when each individual task has limited observations. That is the setting the abstract identifies as common in real-world scenarios: multiple spreading processes occur across similar networks, but no single network is observed enough to support confident standalone inference. The reported experiments on synthetic and real-world networks claim higher inference accuracy than existing techniques while maintaining high computational efficiency. Practically, this buys a way to study hidden spreading routes without waiting for abundant data from every single network. It also makes multi-network evidence useful instead of treating it as unrelated background.
limits: The method depends on the networks being similar in a way the update strategy can exploit. If the networks only look related on the surface but have different spreading pathways, joint inference could transfer misleading structure. The observed diffusion results must also contain enough signal to constrain the hidden networks; shared learning cannot recover routes that leave no trace in any task. The abstract states theoretical monotonicity and convergence, but those guarantees concern the iterative process, not automatic truth of the recovered networks. The experiments cover synthetic and real-world networks, but the abstract does not prove performance under adversarial observations, rapidly changing networks, severe missing data, or cases where the diffusion model itself is misspecified.
